rv.q: The production values alone are a jaw-dropper.
Eva Noblezada has an enormous, poignant strength and a piercing voice that can delicately float as confidently as it blasts.
I was unprepared to be so consistently entertained for the two-and-a-half-hour duration.
Miss Saigon was, and is, a phenomenon, and this production, directed by Laurence Connor, is sensational in every way.
The “gadzooks!” arrival of the helicopter isn’t the only way in which this tale of love, betrayal and sacrifice in the last days of the Vietnam War summons the gaslight era.
Grittier, prettier and yet somehow seeming even more pedestrian than before, “Miss Saigon” has redeployed to Broadway, making lots of noise but managing to say precious little.
But then the unrelieved hyperemphasis of Laurence Connor’s direction basically squashes whatever might be good in Miss Saigon.
While “Miss Saigon” has a can’t-miss plot—it’s as potent today as it was for Puccini—the score, at least to my ear, is unendurable.
In terms of musical bombast, visual spectacle and hyperbolic vulgarity, it closed out a sad decade for the serious American musical.
Connor’s direction brings this one home, making the themes, especially the plight of the refugees, feel very contemporary.
Oh yes, "Miss Saigon" soars to the rafters.

"'Miss Saigon' is more relevant and heartbreaking today than when it premiered on Broadway in 1991...As directed by Laurence Connor, this solid and satisfying revival builds on the extraordinary visuals, nonstop adrenaline, sweeping emotions and pulsating musical score that characterized the original production while adding an unmissable brutali...
Judging from the packed theater, it might well sing Claude-Michel Schönberg's soaring melodies and wow audiences with its spectacular staging for another decade.
The new Miss Saigon is as hypnotic in its storytelling as it is overwrought in depicting its small tale of five people caught up in events beyond their control.

When you look beyond the hulking scenery and American Idol-style glory notes, you can see Miss Saigon for what it really is: a bruising indictment of American self-pity in an age in which we still control the lion's share of wealth and power.
It's an evening of big Broadway, with music that will move you and set pieces that will thrill.
The helicopter scene remains phenomenal.
It mars the show's otherwise fine-tuned return.
This production, while dated, is not without tooth, and at its best moments, usually in its big production numbers, it can still deliver plenty of bite.

"Never much rises above the level of hummable schmaltz. Yet if 'Miss Saigon' hasn't necessarily refined with age, this is nonetheless a handsome, accomplished production—an artful application of lipstick on a pot-bellied pig.
Eva Noblezada, this production's Kim, makes her Broadway debut and is probably the show's biggest wow (sorry, helicopter).
Still, if you're a fan of 'Miss Saigon,' this is a first-class revival, both in terms of its cast and production values.

"The production’s impressive visual spectacle, lively staging and crowd-pleasing vocal calisthenics cannot completely mask a script that leans heavily on emotional manipulation and one-dimensional storytelling...Perhaps a miraculous cast could take such blunt-force emotional instruments and soften them into credibility...
But this is a bright, Broadway spectacular where the grit and hard facts of history are impossible to ignore, or square with Miss Saigon’s song-and-dance, flashy sets and flashing lights.
Admittedly, I suspect the crowds may still eat up this misbegotten musical, but I found a second helping of this show awfully hard to swallow.
Once again the music is merely loud when it needs to be affecting.
Maybe Miss Saigon could get away with such blatant racism in 1991, but in 2017 the musical feels more problematic than loveable.
With its lush and melodic score, “Miss Saigon” remains an ambitious and stunningly effective musical even as it also borders on the overwhelming.
With a top-notch cast, dynamic visuals, and a story that speaks to the complexities of the American Dream, this classic will definitely be beloved by a new generation of theatergoers.
The result is a mediocre production, waffling between dirty and gritty, and polished and sensational, never committing to either.
Miss Saigon just isn't my bag--really, megamusicals in general just don't do it for me, but that's not to say that the production isn't done very, very well.
This production truly takes the objectification of women to a new level of inappropriateness.
Miss Saigon uses spectacle to manufacture tragedy, forgetting the human element along the way.
But, unfortunately, when politics meets soap opera, soap opera wins. The show now seems sentimental, dated.
Instead, we're left to question why it's returned as though it never left, without anything more to say.

cn.t: This bombastic revival impresses with spectacular production values and strong performances, but critics remain divided on its dated, melodramatic storytelling and problematic Orientalist clichés.

vs.sum: The Broadway Theatre's vast size (1,761 seats) and exceptional depth mean rear orchestra and balcony seats are very far from the stage, making it best suited to large-scale spectacle productions. The Renaissance-inspired interior is grand, though comfort is below average with tight seating.

acc.note: 7 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. Infrared devices available.
